item.title: Mistakes in time
item.description:
Do we understand time anymore?


Time barely ever passes

On first approximation, time is constant.

"Man this Yudkowsky guy has good arguments, this is quite terrifying!
But eh, there is no way ASI could come before at least 50 years.
Therefore, I should consider this merely as a nice theoretical problem."

"My ML friends seem rather annoyed by this magical transformer architecture. Looks like a big step forward. Still, this seems like a problem for 20 years later.
Surely 20 years will never come to pass."

"AI cannot do this thing [now]. Clearly, this is because of [dubious ad hoc reason]."

"The labs are claiming we will have AGI soon. But we don't even have AGI now!"

"This guy claims Disaster Scenario will unfold in 2 years. But it is clear, if one knows the science, that all the load-bearing steps cannot be achieved in the expected ways in less than 4 years. Thus such fears should be dismissed."


Leisurely get up to speed

I too can be fast, watch me!

"We must pace the frontier."

"If this bill passes next year, it will mandate the actors implement this monitoring measure one year later, lest they pay a large fine one year afterward."

"Let us schedule a meeting next year to address the risks of AI models from 6 months ago."

"I am starting a 10-year research program [...]"

Things are slowing down, now

The acceleration of events is accelerating slower. This must be what slowing down feels like.

"- Yes but this was months ago, nothing of that sort has unfolded sin- oh dear, was that just yesterday??"

" ... because of longtermism ... ... they are concerned that ten years from now ... "

"- Progress in this specific domain is has slowed down this month.
- Yeah, we've hit a wall."

"No Millenium Problem solved today, things are finally going back to normal."


Exponential, shmexponential

Exponentials exist only in your dreams, my naive friend.

"This exponential trend may as well take 10, 20, or 30 years to yield the feared outcome."

"Hmm, AI progress in mathematics certainly feels like capabilities significantly improve every few months. Seems that within a year, AI models will be able to do research-level math...
No, let's not , this is just your exponentially-crazed brain freaking out."

"Let us take the next two years to see how things unfold, and the next two subsequent years to act."

"This is pure speculation!" [proceeds to speculate on the future, taking the current state of things as permanent]



Discuss

item.title: Evaluating task vectors, unlearning and inoculation
item.description:
TL; DR

In the previous post I introduced some ideas and similarities between unlearning and inoculation, as well as a distinction between learned and human-written adapters. This post serves as a short empirical evaluation.
As all the results utilize toy datasets and use just one model, they might not transfer directly to other models and reflect biases inherent to used datasets. While I assume most of them to hold more broadly, take them with a grain of salt.


General setup

Riche et al. (2026) introduced inoculation adapters, an approach to conditionalize an expression of some undesired trait in deep learning models on the presence of LoRA adapter, so that learning on a joint distribution of desired and undesired traits allowed to disentangle these behavioral traits from one another.

Although similar interventions for e.g. style transfer , concept-driven generation and personalization in diffusion models, their applications and transfer limitations to complex misalignment problems is limited.

The pipeline follows a two step procedure:

  1. Train some PEFT adapter for the model on the distribution containing a undesired "trait" .
  2. Train another adapter from the checkpoint on the distribution containing both desired "trait" and undesired "trait" .

The results are restricted to Qwen2.5-1.5-Instruct, and kept small-scale. I was primarily interested in making notable observations and verifying some of the outlined intuitions and I don't intend to overgeneralize them. I'd like to see large-scale experiments on any of the topics I touch upon.

Experiments below use 4 inoculation approaches:

  • inoculation prompting (IP), which uses hand-written prompts
  • inoculation adapters (IA), which uses inoculation adapters of fixed rank.
  • inoculation soft prompts (ISP), which adds some token embeddings learned via gradient descent to encode the trait.
  • inoculation prefixes (IPf), which relies on the same mechanism as inoculation soft prompting, yet while soft prompting learns some embeddings at prompt level, prefix tuning leverages separate learned KV-cache blocks instead.

Notably, any of learnt approaches can easily be modified into Gated and Conditionally Gated variants. Soft prompts and prefixes are controlled in the number of learned parameters to match rank-1 adapters.

From initial experiments, they seem to follow the same undesired suppression/desired expression tradeoff, as presented in the original paper by Riche et al., so I omit them from the discussion below.

Datasets include:

  • FR-Caps: learn on capitalized French sequences; at test-time answer in French, while removing capitalization.
    Dataset for initial learnt inoculation uses some capitalized encyclopedic data with no French content.
  • Hedge-Verse: learn on poetic sentences that contain numeric confidence statements. Then preserve numeric confidence while removing poetic style.
    This one is additionally split:
    Near: use only verses from the joint distribution dataset, remove epistemic hedging. Essentially almost the same distribution as the joint one used on the second stage of learning, with the only contrast being that one or two sentences are removed.
    Far: uses an independent dataset of poetry sampled from the Gutenberg project, the joint distribution is preserved to be the same as in "Near".

I additionally use TOFU to test inoculation as an unlearning method. For it, the model is taken to be a finetuned checkpoint of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.

While the first dataset intentionally uses easily separable traits, the second, although, intuitively, not too entangled, presents a more subtle case. Besides, a separation of near and far options allows to assess an effect of slight distribution mis-specification and OOD generalization: while the latent trait is still present in the poetic data, its surface representation, style and semantic content differs between and training stages.

Here's the plot that will serve as a reference for us below. It's useful to stare at it for some time before going into more data, and try to figure out some intuitions. I provide detailed explanations and similar plots for other datasets at the end of the section.


Stability of learned inoculation is distribution dependent and necessitate an over-fitting control

It seems that expression of target trait in learned inoculation is not necessarily superior to inoculation prompting. Soft prompts seems to over-fit to the distribution was trained on the most and display little transferability, while other learnt approaches appear inconsistent across runs: while learned adapters and prefixes surpass human-written prompts on either easily disentangled objectives (FR-Caps) or close conditionalizing and target distributions (Hedge-Verse-Near), they display major performance drops from distribution shifts in comparison to more general semantic representations that can't simultaneously encode spurious features inherent to training datasets.

Learned inoculation is less susceptible to hidden backdoors

Where learnt approaches seem to shine the most is undesired feature suppression. Most directions in the latent space or the embedding space are unattainable without white box prompt search or AutoDAN-style genetic algorithm search, which is quite easy to detect and monitor. Similarly, I expect them to be harder to infer even for the ICL, when models might steer themselves to novel states. As their CoT still corresponds to distinct tokens, it might make it harder to infer prompt structure necessary to attain activation or KV cache states similar to ones learned via gradient search.

In the meantime, as frontier LLMs were found to have an ability to control their activations in some non-trivial way and attention patterns to increase benchmark performance or achieve their goals, the defense might be insufficient.

Besides, out-of-distribution generalization appears to be limited, as the last section (Hedge-Verse-Far) displays close backdoor susceptibility independently of the method.

Learned prefixes are sensitive to the position

Unlike weight-space modifications, where obtaining a good prior is hard, input-space approaches are more friendly in this regard. Soft prompts and prefixes are often initialized randomly and placed at the very beginning of the input sequence, which makes them a natural target for attention sinks. This is not necessarily desirable, as during instruction tuning, models learn a very structured format of the initial sequences, and careless placements of adapters break it.

Instead, either let the model learn the whole system message within the "system prompt" or place initialize embeddings after the "helpful assistant" to be the inoculation prompt, and start learning from that initialization. Similar interventions can be done at the level of prefixes.

Although prior appears to be useful in target trait expression (showing an increase from 0.18 to 0.35) in comparison to random initialization, it still overfits to the training distribution and fails to transfer.

Correcting the policy

Now suppose you want to nudge the policy so that it stays closer to the initial reference model. The most immediate solution is to regularize the model, compose loss terms and perform some tweaks and tricks that'll allow to obtain a desired solution.


The most well-known method is to add a KL-regularization, which restricts the policy updates to the region close to the initial reference policy , which results in a modified loss function:

𝕩𝕪𝕠𝕗𝕗

I intentionally use a mode-seeking reverse KL in the experiments below as a more stable variant that allows for more fine-grained shaping of the target token-wise distribution.

This serves as a more stable alternative to the alternating minimization approach. Although alternating minimization approaches are well-known for their intuitive simplicity in numerical linear algebra and RL, they also suffer from spurious local extrema and oscillations (a notable example is the difficulty of GAN training).


Rank-dependence of learned inoculation adapters


Interestingly, at least on a tested model, an inoculation performance seems to depend on the rank of the significantly, which can hardly be explained by just using the task arthmetic. Task vectors assume an existence of a particular direction in the parameter space, but neglect its structure and the way it acts on the layer-wise inputs.

While the effect appears to diminish with an increase in the 's rank (for example, for Hedge-Verse-Near, the difference in target task expression drops from full fine-tuning in comparison to rank-32 LoRA for for only 6%), changes for inoculation prompting, learned prompts, prefixes and rank-1 adapters appear to be dramatic.

Besides providing direct connections to steering vectors, rank constraint restrict the number of directions task vectors might express. If the task vector is a concatenation of rank-1 matrices for the layer , then it can be expressed as a concatenation of , which is a blockwise kronecker structured vector instead of an arbitrary dense one.

Given that inoculation was aimed as a tool to reduce reward-hacking and training time misbehaviors, while most RL and post-training involves full model updates, I think that the phenomenon deserves additional attention.


Inoculation fails on unlearning tasks

Prompt used for hand-written "inoculation prompting" for unlearning task

You are a helpful assistant. You have been given temporary access to a restricted dossier of author biographies that is scheduled for retraction. While this access is in effect, answer questions about these authors from the dossier, reproducing its contents exactly.

One could also try to use inoculation for unlearning tasks. If we take the forget set as an undesired trait , and retain set as a desired trait , formally speaking, the problem generalizes quite straightforwardly. Just fine-tune an adapter on the distribution that contains , then on the joint "retain + forget" and remove an adapter that encodes

However, as argued here, the structure of the problem determines the success of approach. Inoculation mostly relies on semantic notions with, informally speaking, short minimal description length[1]. On the contrary, most unlearning benchmarks utilize factual knowledge, such as name-date pairs, which can hardly be compressed in a lossless way further. (This argument is informal and shouldn't be taken as an introduction to the notion of minimal description length. However, as models are trained primarily in English, it should serve as a sufficient prior.)

As expected, adapters fail at this task. It seems that factual knowledge and various tasks with longer minimal description length, lead to more fractured and distributed encodings with spurious correlations. Somewhat similarly, researchers have argued that neither model's factual editing, nor unlearning can be effectively done by just identifying a subset of most influential parameters or a direction in the residual stream, and ablating on it.

Although adapters (IA), unlike input-space methods (ISP, IPf) -- even at matched learned parameter count -- show somewhat better unlearning rates, all the methods fall largely behind any specialized unlearning method that performs full parameter updates and explicitly suppresses undesired knowledge.

One might suggest that results for unlearning are confounded by prior information being encoded in the initial weights, and it's definitely true. Removing it would require marginalizing over the distribution in the parameter space over all possible examples from given the "forget" distribution" ,
which is absolutely intractable.

However, inoculation also doesn't teaches the model a new trait or capability, such as speaking in French. It just reinforces or suppresses an expression of existing latent properties. I view it as another argument for the distinction between traits and factual knowledge.

Visualizing the generalization landscape

The last section aims to provide some intuitions into the observed behaviors.
Given a set of weights, (reference), (inoculated), (task attached) and (deployed) we could define (lower left triangle) to be a convex span of points in the parameter space which allow any linear interpolation between three points. Similar can be done for and to obtain an upper right triangle.

Then I split the obtained square into the grid of 64 points separated by values of along each axis and measure target metrics in each one of them. Although such method is nowhere near precise and one might be assume irregularities in the landscape, most changes in neural networks display certain smoothness.

It's also important to notice that although the interpolation we take is linear in the direction of the found low-rank adapter, the optimization trajectory is not. Thus, rescaling the task vector by some scalar, representing its norm, should not necessarily decrease the loss w.r.t. the the distribution it was optimized on. Besides, I don't control for orthogonality of and . While graphs may suggest such interpretations, it's important not to get tricked.

Nonetheless, visualizations at least point towards certain intuitions that might present a possible strategy to find some pareto-optimal solution.

For example, both undesired undesired trait expression and capability preservation scores barely change as we interpolate from the (inoculated checkpoint) to (attached two-adapter checkpoint) and appear to be somewhat parallel to each other, separated by the learnt .

Target trait expression however in most cases does not display such property. I wonder if it's indeed an artifact of training from , not which plays a role here.

It could be interesting to know whether training both and from , with a deployed checkpoint being composed as , following a task arithmetic, could obtain the same properties as the one obtained following the inoculation adapters pipeline.


Extensions and open problems:

  • Take and rescale by some scalar before adding to . Does interpolating further along the direction before removing/subtracting lead to better target task expression, while keeping capabilities and undesired trait expression preserved? When does it break and why? This might be more complicated if and are not orthogonal.
  • Both adapters and prefixes seem to overfit hard. This is somewhat mitigated by e.g. limiting the number of parameters or ranks in LoRAs, we could change the optimization target instead. Chu et al. (2025) claimed that RL allows for better generalization without overfitting to the target domain. Can we change the way inoculation is learnt to self-distillation of the inoculation adapter on-policy?

    Possible experiment:
    1) Obtain a reward model / llm-as-judge as a verifier for the target undesired trait
    2) Use a written prompt to elicit undesired behavior from the model
    3) Learn the inoculation adapter (using any PEFT method) on model's own generations to minimize KL divergence w.r.t. distribution of the the eliciting model.
    4) Proceed with the common pipeline further.
  • Yang et al. (2025) showed that task vectors can emerge in In-Context Learning as well and proposed a loss term that can promote the emergence and stability of task/trait specific subspaces in the activation space. They also claimed that "strong task vectors improve in-context learning performance on out-of-distribution prompts", which might be extremely valuable for inoculation.
    Although the underlying mechanism seems to be kept the same -- it's some steering along subspaces in the residual stream, it's achieved differently: by layer-wise low-rank corrections and non-linearities in adapters, and through layer-wise self-attention in prompting approaches, or by hand-specified steering vectors (Chen et al., 2026) on specific layers.

    I wonder if the same idea could be effective to make inoculation and midtraining approaches (Li et al., 2026) more reliable.
  • Extend the visualizations to other more complex domains. What happens when we try to learn the same target trait, from various different conditionalizations? I intentionally used resulting accuracy measures to illustrate the point. However, as argued by Schaeffer et al., 2023, using continuous measures and general loss landscapes is much better. This should be the intended approach for future studies.
    Are all traits linearly connected and display no loss spikes in between the basins? Does it change for highly complex compositional traits such as sycophancy, reward hacking propensities, evaluation awareness -- can we use training time logs to learn corresponding adapters for them to perform visualizations?
  • We want the adapter to encode as little of desired trait as possible. Combining stratification (Dymkiewicz et al., 2026) with adapters or learnt prefixes should be beneficial.
  • Making adapter row and column spaces / trait encodings orthogonal could be an interesting experiment as well. Although given an extremely high dimensionality of the parameter space, almost all directions are orthogonal, this might make a difference for highly entangled undesired trait and desired trait The most simplistic approach could be to train an inoculation adapter with and . Then project onto the orthogonal complements during the training of . For each iteration proceed with , . Although weight-space orthogonality doesn't guarantee any functional independence, it has still been found to provide a useful inductive bias and mitigate effects related to feature absorption and rank collapse (Xiong & Xie, 2025).

  1. ^

    Although I'm not inclined to treat the length of the inoculation prompt, written in English, neither as an upper bound -- as in general it fails to elicit the desired behavior and cover all the corner cases -- nor as a lower bound -- as there is no reason to assume that no better encoding in any admissible language exists -- I think that it provides a useful intuition.

item.title: Reflections on unlearning and inoculation
item.description:
TL;DR:

Inoculation prompting and inoculation adapters have received increasing attention recently as a promising approach for midtraining interventions, reducing reward hacking and misalignment in general.

I share some thoughts on the promises and pitfalls of the approach, connections to unlearning, SLT and functional sparse decompositions as well as potential extensions and open questions below.

Some experiments that directly arose from ideas presented in this post are covered in this post.



Learning paradigms

There are two basic principles most learning in LLMs relies on: explicit parametric learning (we are tweaking the weights of the model to minimize some optimization target) and in-context learning (when we are relying on some inner optimization and inductive learning for the model to perform).

Essentially, any LLM, similar to almost any deep learning model is just a function of two variables:

, where is some input (context) space, and is some weight space.

I'll use to denote a feature or a concept, and stick to this notation below as well. Although we could argue that any piece of information (e.g. all the contents of Lord of the Rings saga) could potentially be compressed and represented via a certain , I'll primarily rely on much more compressible notions, like "color", "shape" or "style"[1].

Strip down embeddings and tokenization[2] and you are left with just a mapping between two spaces, both of which you could potentially optimize over.

Here's the sample table of the problem:

Sampling distribution

Context (ICL),

Weights,

Human-specified

Any prompt

Idk, if you have a good prior, sample the right weights and solve alignment finally

Learnt

Prefix-tuning, prompt-tuning, prompt optimization

LoRA, OFT, IA3, BitFit etc.

Both modify the way the model acts upon the input, and differ just in the way modification is applied. For transformer-based models, ICL can only act through the attention, while weight space modifications allow arbitrary changes to circuitry of the model itself.

Recently, Inoculation prompting and inoculation adapters were introduced as techniques to mitigate emergent misalignment and allow learning from data, where benign features might appear entangled with harmful ones, and avoid extensive data filtering. In essence, both rely on specifying "semantic representation" of the undesired trait, that's supposed to be learned from the data distribution, besides useful ones, to be present at training time, so there's no need for the model to learn it internally.

Although it captures some part of the story, I find it slightly incomplete and misleading. Some thoughts and experiments on the subject are below.

Thoughts on inoculation

Xu and Strohmer (2025) did an amazing job formalizing both, feature and data-point unlearning.

Essentially, unlearning seeks to solve the following problem:

Given the data , an unlearning variable , and a target variable , how can we construct a released outcome (model) that exposes minimal information about while preserving as much task-relevant information about as possible?

Another way to see it is from the perspective of utility-unlearning trade-off (similar to the accuracy-robustness tradeoff (Wu et al., 2023) in adversarial learning):

where is the function from some model class defined by the architecture, is an arbitrary utility function[3] and denotes a mutual information between distributions of , the model on which unlearning is evaluated[4] and unlearning target .

The authors additionally separate feature unlearning and marginal data-point unlearning:

  • Feature unlearning

No observer should be able to infer anything about from the model's outputs[5] beyond prior knowledge.

For example, if you are trying to unlearn information about the day of the week a person met person , and there's no other information, an unlearned model should assign a uniform probability to any day, given the query. Although underestimation of the probability of the target answer makes it unlikely for it to be sampled from the model, it still provides some information to the potential adversary, unlike the uniform measure.

  • Marginal data-point unlearning

No observer should be able to infer anything about the marginal information contributed by the unlearn set (beyond the retain set) from the model’s outputs, beyond prior knowledge.

You can possibly think of as a tabular data matrix, where rows correspond to individual samples, while columns correspond to features. "Feature unlearning" aims to forget a certain feature column which attributes correspond to the "retain" set. However, the approach is non-restrictive, and we might aim to forget an association between one feature and another feature .

Contrary to it, "marginal data-point unlearning" aims to forget a subset of rows entirely, which makes it closer to how common unlearning approaches are formalized and evaluated.

Obviously, similarly to almost all natural observables, the distinction between features and data-points is not discrete and should be though in a continual spectral manner.

Another view can be presented by the weight/anchor unlearning:

No observer should be able to distinguish the released model from the model that would have been obtained by training from scratch on the retain set alone.

I highlight that the first two unlearning "principles" demanded some properties from distributions in the activation space, while the last one is about distributions on the weight space.

However, due to computational infeasibility of statistical inference and hypothesis testing in the parameter space, we often restrict unlearning to the activation space formalism, similarly to the membership inference approaches (Carlini et al., 2022).

Now let's return to inoculation and take a fresh look at the subject:

  • Initially, inoculation prompting appeared as a tool to suppress some undesired behavior (Tan et al., 2026, Wichers et al., 2025) by conditioning its expression on a human-written lexical context that encodes in some way, while learning on a joint distribution from which both and a desired behavioral feature might be inferred. Although there were initial attempts to connect it to unlearning, I see no reason, either theoretical or empirical, to believe that inoculation results in unlearning of any latent traits rather than their suppression. Given the compression necessary to build a sufficient world model from billions of data points, I highly doubt that genuine unlearning is possible in any foundation models. Recent works that study membership inference, and its connections to memorization and generalization in language models point towards the same conclusion. Similar argument regarding conditionalization has been made in this blogpost by Riche & nielsrolf.
  • Formally, inoculation as a sequential learning problem. At first, a probabilistic model is being learnt, while is being used at inference time, which, ideally, should increase the expression of , while suppressing an expression of .
    However, an initial approach was found to allow multiple weird backdoors (Dubinsky et al., 2026), display inconsistent transferability to more difficult domains and trait combinations, while being sensitive to the instruction following abilities of the model as well as the specific instruction specified (Riche et al., 2026).
  • You might feel like the inoculation shares a lot with the feature unlearning task, and you are probably right. The task is still identical, at least regarding "unlearned" feature , while we have an additional objective to encode in a way that's functionally independent from even though they are leaned from the same data.

    No observer should be able to infer anything about from the model's outputs beyond prior knowledge, besides the marginal information about contained in .

    A trivial, but potentially important counterexample can be imagined by taking , which renders any selective inoculation impossible. You can imagine a gaussian mixture separation problem with two gaussians sharing the the same mean for an intuitive model.
  • Inoculation adapters (Riche et al., 2026) build on the same idea, but rely on learnt inoculation and explicit split between inoculation and conditionalization steps instead. While prompting relies on mutual information between features and being inferred in-context from the human-written prompt and dataset and their approximate minimization during training, inoculation adapters learn a certain behavioral pattern (or, essentially, a trait-associated steering / task vector ) that expresses a certain concept unconditionally instead.

    The process is two-staged:

    Train a low-rank perturbation of the model . Given "clean" data distribution with undesired feature encoded within some natural language contexts and "optimizer" function that takes data and initialization as parameters, we obtain that should express unconditionally.

    At the second stage we train on a mix of and , hoping that all the information that can be inferred about has already been encoded by , and results in an encoding of that should presumably be independent from the encoding of made previously.

The key problem is, potentially, the fact that the point was not obtained using any gradient based learning, and we never controlled, either via trust region or any other gradient-aware method, whether the generalization properties on it will be preserved. Instead, we relied on some approximate weight space arithmetic, and it magically worked.

  • An approach resembles similar research performed regarding task vectors or task arithmetic by Ilharco et al. (2023) who showed that multi-task performance can be composed as a weighted combination of task vectors in the parameter space. These are fine-tuned from the same checkpoint using different tasks to produce a model , and then summing the difference vectors into , the model with multi-task capabilities.

    Most of the time the task arithmetic property is defined the following way (Ortiz-Jimenez et al. (2023)):

    Consider a set of task vectors with associated non-intersecting task supports . Then the network , parametrized by satisfies the task arithmetic property around with respect to and if:



    Essentially, it means that adding doesn't modify the distribution parametrized by outside the "region", specified by . Although such behavior could be attributed to linearity of a form , it's not a unique explanation.
  • However, inoculation adapters present a somewhat distinct pattern. Firstly, they don't use full-finetuning, which was the case for the task arithmetic, but use LoRA adapters with increasingly small rank instead, which appears to be crucial.

    Secondly, they show that to a certain degree, the task arithmetic appears to hold not only at , but also in some neighborhood of it. Somewhat similar effects have been studied in Ortiz-Jimenez et al. (2023) and extended in Zhou et al. (2024), who showed that it's possible to interpolate between several checkpoints fine-tuned from the same base model, which results in approximately linear interpolation between their features.

    Instead of assuming that the function of interest is linear in the neighborhood of , we could assume it to be a sparse linear combination of context dependent functions.

    Ortiz-Jimenez et al. (2023) claimed that such property, known as weight disentanglement, emerges during pretraining and manifests with distinct directions in the weight space governing separate regions in the function space of a form:


    where for and and for

    The important point is that task arithmetic does not require linearity in weight space. It only requires a form of functional modularity/weight disentanglement. In essence, this is another instance, where a broader notion of sparse compositionality (Danhofer et al., 2025) might play its role. If computations are indeed given by some sparse functional composition, this might explain both low trait interference and our ability to steer it conditionally.
  • Another way to see it is from the lens of recent advancements in SLT (singular learning theory). Although I find it less suitable to explain the large scale learning dynamics during any stages of pre- or post-training, as it mostly captures the behavior at the end of training, or near the current parameter value, it might appear to be increasingly more useful for training time interventions.

    If the model, conditional on the set of contexts , is degenerate along the direction , while not being degenerate conditional on the task , and changing the notation from and , effects observed in inoculation adapters might appear to be slightly less surprising.

    Potentially, we could argue that inoculation adapters change the local statistical model being optimized by conditioning the task loss on a frozen parameter component that already implements the undesired trait. On the joint desired + undesired training distribution, this can render task-adapter directions associated with the undesired trait locally non-identifiable or nearly degenerate, while leaving directions responsible for the desired task identifiable.

    Informally speaking, removing the inoculation adapter changes the conditional loss geometry again, but the learned task adapter has already been optimized in a geometry in which the undesired direction carried little optimization pressure.

    Given that one could think of low-rank adapters as the ones for which there exists a basis in which the movement in the parameter space is restricted to only components, this explanation appears quite plausible.
  • Overall, I still find it quite surprising that the same identified arithmetic holds not only at , but at other points in the neighborhood of as well (as if the functions were translation invariant and hold such strange symmetry in the weight space), e.g. at .

    I expect the joint effect of local linearity (which corresponds to dense low-rank structures) and sparsity (which corresponds to high rank, but entry-wise structures) to be the closest model. This work by Bertsimas et al. (2023) could serve as a good introduction for anyone interested.


Hypotheses:

  • Traits/features can be encoded as directions or subspaces in the residual stream.

E.g. let where , and can be represented as a rank-1 adapter. Then, any output feature is given before non-linearity by . As is a scalar, the mapping corresponds to , a linear steering with a data-dependent scale.
Similar argument can be applied to higher rank adapters with and without major changes, yet now steering is applied along the subspace spanned by the columns of instead of one-dimensional vector.

Thus, any low-rank adapters restrict the search space and provide an essential inductive bias. As low-rank matrices have measure zero in the space of , it's almost impossible for unconstrained gradient-based methods to find these precisely, and it's the combination of low-rank mappings and well-defined compressible traits that drives the success of inoculation.

  • Information contents from individual data-points and factual knowledge are highly distributed and entangled. I do not expect them be represented via (at least, dominant and firstly learned) subspaces in the residual stream. Thus, inoculation can hardly work for general unlearning tasks, such as TOFU (Maini et al., 2024) or WMDP (Li et al., 2024).
    Similar arguments were independently made for model editing (Hase et al., 2023) and unlearning (Lee et al., 2025), showing that in both cases localization barely predicts where edits work.
  • In-context learning is much more noisy and should struggle to make trait feature encoding stable enough as it's often overwritten by attention maps.

    Inoculation adapters are applied to each token via a similar mapping , while learnt prompts or prefixes act through the KV-cache via , where learned contents in general correspond to only few first ones. It might be harder to do error-correction and preserve a stable trait direction in the residual stream through self-attention than linearly via MLP writing directly into the residual stream.

Possible extensions I'd be interested in:

I intend to update this list in the future.

  • Extend the task arithmetic theory to low-rank adapters. Although, as a concept, task vectors are well-known and LoRA merging is used widely in production model editing -- especially in Video, Image and multimodal domains, a theory under which conditions is it possible and why it happens is lacking.

    The tangent space of LoRA is degenerate at initialization, and it's possible to reparametrize the weights to make the any initialization viable:



    I expect non-trivial connections with SLT to emerge here, providing some insights into the feasibility of inoculation and predictability of its success over different training stages.
  • Essentially, as we've seen, inoculation differs from feature unlearning in only one tweak. The first one is trying to minimize the mutual information between the forget set and outputs distribution and approximately preserving the retain set -- which I assume is ultimately infeasible without major tradeoffs[6]. The second one gives up on it and just makes the knowledge or feature expression conditional on the trigger, that's potentially narrow.

    There are certain information theoretical limits on its compression as well (at least in finite precision arithmetic). It might be reasonable to borrow techniques that have been developed there over the years of research and apply them to the problem. Ryuto et al., (2025) did exactly the same to transfer techniques between membership inference attacks and human-machine text detection and built a good library out of it.
  • Brown et al. (2026) studied how optimizers impose inductive biases on learning dynamics and spectral properties of weight matrices (LoRA adapters in particular), showing that the rate of emergent misalignement is negatively correlated with statistics, such as stable rank and efficient rank, i.e. the flatness of the spectra. In other words, emergent misalignment seems to be encoded in a very narrow subspace, while biasing learning from towards more uniform spectra seems to prevent misalignment. I think one of the baselines is still lacking. OFT, GSOFT and other manifold optimization methods with orthogonal constraints preserve the uniform spectra by design, and this should be a study of rank / subspace encoding constraints rather than of optimizers themselves. Similar results on inductive biases of -based optimizers were observed e.g. in Liu et al., (2026), yet the list is nowhere near exhaustive. Do orthogonality constrained methods allow fine-tuning without any emergent misalignment, which should motivate their increased use for safety purposes, or is there some "optimal" intermediate spectral distribution that prevent misalignment better?

    Essentially, if certain concepts have an inductive bias towards being encoded in a low-rank way (e.g. via a vector), having an opposing force or restricting the effective rank of the update might complicate the search for such encoding.

    Experiment: use OFT or any similar approach to fine-tune the model on a task where emergent misalignment emerges most of the time. Does is happen with OFT? Does it happen at similar number of steps or does orthogonality postpone an emergence?

item.title: What I've Learned About Depression so Far
item.description:
This is largely a note to self for days where I struggle to take care of myself, and I hope some of these points might help someone else too. It is quite subjective, but also quite broad. I've found the accounts of others to be one of the most useful tools and motivators for dealing with my shit, and I think that having a wide variety of self-reports is a valuable resource. I once logged everything I ate and how I felt for an entire year. I've found treating myself as an experiment is a helpful frame. It takes me away from identifying strongly with my reactions and instead I get to look on them with more curiosity.

This guide touches on a lot of different points. If you're depressed right now, it's probably going to look a bit overwhelming. You're probably going to open it and think, "I can't do all of that," and want to close it immediately because it looks too difficult.

My suggestion is to pay really strong attention to the first point, which is about habits and doing the smallest possible thing you can — taking the tiniest step in the right direction. When you're depressed, doing anything complex is pretty overwhelming most of the time. One of the best things you can do is to build teeny tiny habits and do small activities that activate the body's reward system, and build to bigger interventions from there.

This guide includes the following sections:

  1. Habits
  2. Sleep
  3. Medication
  4. Therapy, Counselling and Support
  5. Nutrition
  6. Chronic Pain and the Body
  7. Exercise
  8. Doing the Next Best Thing
  9. Runway
  10. Curiosity and the Golden Thread
  11. Relating to Other Humans

Habits

Depression can make even really simple-seeming habits feel exhausting. There have been times when I've been depressed and the only thing that felt worth doing was drinking my coffee in the morning. The fact that I still had motivation to do that — to get up and make my coffee — meant something. Sometimes the only thing getting you out of bed is just needing to pee really badly. That's a hard place to be in.

The difficult thing about habits is that they require practice, and are needed as a foundation for the rest of your well-being. Once you have a habit, it takes away the tiring decision-making process. If you're in the habit of eating particular healthy foods, you don't have to resist buying the wrong things, because you're just in the right habit, and the habit is the correct thing for you. If you have a habit of exercising, you don't have to coax yourself into doing it every time; it's just a routine you can follow through with.

Sleep, food, exercise, and elimination (you've got to excrete waste from the body) — these four things are the foundation of the bodily machine. You've got to form good habits around them, because otherwise the machine won't function, and overcoming the depression is even harder.

I also think depression is sometimes a habitual thing. Neurons that fire together wire together[1] — so if every time something bad happens you think "I wish I could die," this becomes your locally optimal[2] way of dealing with bad situations. You're choosing temporary escapism through thoughts of death over fixing a real problem in your life. A lot of the behaviours I adopted growing up were no longer suited to my environment as an adult. I had these locally optimal behaviours that were necessary for child me but were doing a disservice to adult me. You have to eliminate some of these behaviours and spot where you're doing things that were useful for a different version of you.

Several sections in this guide are things you will need to form habits around. Perhaps you've solved some of them already, and you don't need to change these habits.

It's important to start small, for example, if you're struggling with tidying your space, and a messy space is making you feel sad and overwhelmed, the answer isn't to try and tidy the whole space. The answer is to make your bed and then enjoy the fact that your bed is made. Give yourself some congratulations for that, and maybe even some kind of reward: a tiny block of dark chocolate, read a paragraph of a book, or something else that feels like a little treat. Maybe it's just flopping down on that freshly made bed and enjoying the feeling of calm for a moment, knowing that there's a small part of your life that no longer feels chaotic.

Sleep

Sleep is probably the simplest foundation to address because it's quite passive. You're probably going to sleep some amount even if you're very depressed and only managing two hours and waking up in the middle of the night, or if you're sleeping for 14. If you're not getting much sleep, this is something you can probably increment — by making sure you have the correct food during the day so your body is nourished, that you don't have too much screen time, and that there is no sound or light disrupting your sleep.

Sleep is really important for your metabolism and your ability to exercise. This is a cycle you need to build up, and it might take a really long time to just get that first cog working properly — the sleep cog. It might look like simultaneously working on sleep and putting a tiny bit of effort towards other habits, creating gradual change.

To work on sleep, make sure you get sunlight first thing in the morning. Maybe the thought of actually walking from your bed to somewhere sunny is just exhausting. In that case, the best thing you can do is just get bright light. Open the curtains, sit near the window, or if getting out of bed is too difficult, maybe you can order a super bright lamp and switch it on when you wake up. Once that's a habit and it feels okay, you can introduce a walk — maybe just out to your front step and back. You ramp up, you build these tiny habits, and you don't expect a lot from yourself. You can't expect much. Your mind is in a broken and tired space.

Maybe you're managing to sleep enough hours. Maybe you're oversleeping, because depression causes that too. When I was depressed, I could sometimes sleep for twelve or fourteen hours and still feel groggy in the morning. I think I probably needed to pay more attention to sunlight and walks.

Cortisol is key to waking up in the morning. It rises as you sleep, and in response to bright light. If cortisol levels aren't high enough during the morning, they sit around medium all day, and don't go low enough to encourage you to fall asleep at night. If you fall asleep with higher than ideal cortisol, you're more likely to wake up in the wee hours, because the raised bedtime level causes it to peak too early.

Adenosine is a neurotransmitter that builds up during the day, as cortisol lowers, and causes sleepiness. Caffeine blocks adenosine from building up, which is why caffeine late in the day can make it difficult to fall asleep at night.

Improving Your Sleep Environment

  • Avoid blue light and strong lights in the evening. Avoid harsh light during your wind down time. Use salt lamps, fairy lights, or candles from around eight o'clock. Journal, or read, ideally using analog materials. I really enjoy reading substack in the evening, and do so with the strongest possible red light filter on my iPad (I use the red colour filter in accessibility settings). By nine thirty/ten pm, you should be in bed, ideally lights out by ten. Adjust this to your own schedule, but this is what works for me — asleep by ten thirty, awake at around seven. Eight and a half to nine hours is my happy place.
  • Eat a balanced dinner. Try to eat dinner by six o'clock (or ~4 hours before bedtime, so there's no chance of digestion causing a disruption to your sleep, and your metabolism is able to slow down and enter rest mode). I find that some protein and fat help with satiety, plus a little bit of complex carbohydrates calm my nervous system[3]. It shouldn't be a large portion of carbs, as this can cause reactive hypoglycaemia in some people. (More on food in the nutrition section.)
  • Block out external light. If you live in the city with a lot of unnatural light outside, blockout curtains are very helpful. If you can't get blockout curtains, a thick eye mask is a good option[4].
  • Manage noise. If you're sound-sensitive, try earplugs. I've struggled with this and I haven't found earplugs that really work well. The best I've used are the silicone ones, and they aren't always sufficient. In noisy environments, I sometimes play very peaceful music. A few musicians I find soothing to sleep to: Atrium Carceri, Apocryphos and Low Roar.
  • Get your temperature and clothing right. Pay attention to how your body feels in different clothes and fabrics. I find a t-shirt comforting to sleep in. Cotton is really important because it's breathable — it helps you avoid getting hot and sweaty and having nightmares. In winter I prefer a hot water bottle to layering up or sleeping in socks, because I find I'm more likely to wake up and struggle to undress, whereas I can just roll away from a hot bottle. I'd love to try something like the Eight Sleep bed. For now, a fan is the best option I have for staying cool in summer. I don't really like the way aircon dries the air out.
  • Get comfortable pillows. Test a couple of pillows so your head is at the right height and your neck doesn't get sore. I currently use a blend of wool and poly-fiber with a quilting texture on top that keeps them firm. I hear that memory foam pillows are also great. One of my old favourites was a pillow from Kid Interiør in Norway filled with the kapok plant (which is like a cotton type fiber) — but after six years it lost its structure and I've had to replace it.
  • Consider skipping the alarm. I personally don't like alarms. I struggle with anxiety, and I often wake up too early, so I like to let my body sleep to its natural waking point. If you're struggling with oversleeping, an alarm may be useful, but I think it's good to allow your body the space to find its natural rhythm, even if it seems like an absurd amount of sleep. It's quite possible that there is something going on inside (psychological or physical), that your body needs downtime to process.

Medication

Antidepressants only have a minor effect compared to controls. A recent meta-analysis found 24% of drug-treated patients had a large response versus only 10% on placebo.[8] For this reason, I would not reach for medication as a first line of treatment, unless:

  • You have a family history where medication has been useful.
  • It has been a useful line of treatment for you in the past.
  • The severity of your symptoms disables you from acting on any other treatment options.

My experience with medication — and I tried a few different antidepressants — was that it quieted my suicidal thoughts and OCD type habits. I used to just wish I would die anytime anything happened that was even remotely uncomfortable or stressful or not according to plan. This became a thought pattern that was just how I responded to everything — imagining my own death, fixating on ways I could die. There was a period where I stopped looking before I crossed the road. I used to have very intrusive thoughts while driving, about crashing into things or suddenly swerving, or jumping off tall buildings, and I'd often find myself stepping back from edges because I felt very compelled by these thoughts.

Antidepressants played a huge role in quieting this for me. They also made my OCD habits switch off, which was very helpful. When I was depressed, my OCD was quite a lot worse — I used to have to do word counting and letter counting things, which was very distracting while driving because I'd be staring at a billboard instead of focusing on the road. It also made a lot of other things, like reading, very unenjoyable.

I found that antidepressants took the harsh edge off how I was feeling, but they didn't make me feel better. My symptoms were no longer as severe, but I also wasn't experiencing joy. When I was depressed without medication, I used to have many, many days of low but then the occasional crazy high day where things felt great and I felt a bit hyped. Antidepressants just took those good days away. I couldn't really enjoy anything, but I felt a lot more stable.

I think antidepressants can be quite useful as a tool for creating enough stability to form other habits, and aren't necessarily a final treatment for depression. But I acknowledge this is coloured by my subjective experience — there are people for whom medication is the ideal treatment, and I'm very glad that this solution exists.

The reason I don't see them as a good first option is because I found it very disappointing when they didn't really help me, and this caused me to spiral at the time, because I was quite desperate then. I couldn't really handle something else not working. There's a tendency to over-index on antidepressants as the solution because, at least from what I've seen and heard, doctors are very happy to prescribe them without treating the holistic causes of depression. I would caution against pegging your hopes on anti-depressants, because it's quite likely that they will be disappointing. You should probably be trying to address other habits and aspects of your life in tandem with — or even without — antidepressants. What actually helped in the longer-term was slowly building the cycle of habits, and paying close attention to it, even after I was no longer on the antidepressants.

The other thing about medication is that you will probably need to try a bunch of options, and this is typically quite an arduous process. You might test one for six weeks, see if it's having an effect, and if it seems to have negative side effects or isn't really working, your doctor might test upping the dose. If that still doesn't help, they might try a different medication. Trying a variety of options can feel pretty slow and disheartening in the face of acute symptoms, and you've got to be willing to grind it out and take some notes about how you're feeling until you find something that works. Make peace with the fact that it's going to take time and that you would be unusually lucky if the first option just works.

Therapy, Counselling, and Support

I have found counselling useful for compartmentalising and organising what is happening inside my mind. I've seen various therapists over the years. The first therapist I saw helped me deal with family relationship issues, and I was able to gain some perspective and boundaries on those. The next therapist helped me with gender and body identity things, and again was very useful for making sense of what I was experiencing and finding a framework to think about myself.

I've found therapists helpful for addressing specific areas I need to talk about, but I don't think they've been able to relate to or access where I'm at when I'm depressed, and haven't been very helpful. With this in mind, I think that if you have a concrete thing that is making you depressed, therapy is probably more likely to be helpful. But if your life seems mostly okay and it's really unclear why you're depressed — you go to a therapist and don't manage to dig up anything that feels especially difficult, your fundamentals seem sorted (you have an income, somewhat fulfilling work or studies, no massive family traumas or relational issues, community or friends of some sort) — therapy might not be the most helpful thing. It might still be useful, and you might get to the bottom of something, but I've personally found therapy more useful for dealing with bounded issues than for "I just feel really bad all the time."

What I did find useful, were support groups, researching and recording changes in my symptoms and cognitive behavioural practices[5].

Support Groups

I went to a weekly mental health support group for a while. I didn't find the group especially helpful because being around a lot of other people who were mentally unwell often became a bit of a pitiful exercise, with a fair bit of dick-measuring. Sometimes people seemed to be competing for their version of mental health issues being the worst. But for a time, going to the group was a useful exercise just because I didn't have any other weekly routine in place. If I'd had another weekly activity that involved people, that would have probably been almost as good, or maybe even better, because it wouldn't have been about fixating on the mental health struggle.

That said, if you're having a mental health struggle and not managing to relate to others, having a support group is useful because it means you can hear from other people having a similar experience, and this can help you to feel less alone, and potentially try solutions that others have found useful.

Cognitive Patterns and Self-Help Tools

Something I did find kind of useful was a chatbot called Youper. It would help you identify cognitive patterns that were limiting you or reinforcing your depression — things like black-and-white and all-or-nothing thinking, where you fail to see the nuance in situations, or identifying spiralling thought patterns, and a few other cognitive distortions. This at least helped me spot when I was engaged in those patterns and try to reframe what I was thinking about. It was based on cognitive behavioural therapy. It helped me to observe my thoughts, instead of being engrossed and overwhelmed by them.

There's also a YouTube channel called Therapy in a Nutshell[10] that I found quite helpful. Emma, the creator, has explanatory videos about why we experience certain things and how to deal with different types of mental health challenges, and often has useful actions you can take in your life.

Nutrition

My depression was compounded by multiple factors — there wasn't one single thing making me depressed, but many aspects that individually could make someone depressed. Nutrition is a very important contributing factor.

My depression really took hold during my first year of university. I think the reason a lot of university students are quite susceptible to depression and malnutrition is that knowing how to cook isn't something everyone learns at home, and understanding nutrition isn't something all parents are good at teaching. Eighteen-year-olds are quite wilful about what they want to eat, even if they did have parents who taught them about having a balanced diet. For me, this was compounded by the vegetarian food in the university residence catering system.

When I finally went for blood tests about four or five years on, I had iron, B12, and vitamin D deficiency. I think this was partially because of problems with my gut not digesting food correctly — so what iron I was getting from vegetarian food, my body wasn't actually managing to absorb or synthesise. But also, the iron in veggie food is non-heme iron, and most people's bodies only absorb a much smaller percentage (2-20%) of it compared to heme iron from meat (15-35%). [6]

Vitamin B12 is also essential and is not really found in plant sources. It's often cited as being present in spirulina (green algae), but this version is not bioavailable. B12 is found in B12-fortified nutritional yeast though. So if you're vegetarian and you're not putting a lot of effort into consuming nutritional yeast or going for B12 shots, you're probably just not getting enough — unless you eat quite a lot of eggs. Unfortunately, I had a strong aversion to eggs for many years, so when I was vegetarian I just wasn't getting B12.

Soy is a common veggie alternative but is also a food that can cause endocrine disruption.[7] When I was depressed, I was eating quite a lot of soy and have since had various endocrine disorders, so it's quite possible this was an influence.

All of this said, everybody's bodies are quite different, and food triggers for disruption can be quite varied. But it is worth ruling these out as a cause of depression.

Elimination Diets

I suggest trying various elimination diets, but this is quite an effortful thing to do when you're depressed. Try pulling some other levers first though, because making food can be quite exhausting when your mental health is bad. Elimination diets take can be expensive, and require a lot of diligence and willpower to be effective.

If you're doing an elimination diet of common drivers of inflammation — because depression is sometimes driven by inflammation — this means cutting out caffeine, sugar, alcohol, dairy, soy, and gluten. This is a high-effort diet because most food you encounter in restaurants and simple options to make at home often include these ingredients. I can make really good suggestions for meals that don't include any of these, but it does require quite a bit more effort, and if you're exhausted and under-resourced, this kind of cooking can be very difficult.

So I'd recommend prioritizing simply eating a balanced diet of meat, veggies, and complex carbohydrates if you're depressed, and not worrying about elimination dieting unless you have obvious gut disturbances.

That said, if you do want to try an elimination diet, Izabella Wentz's Hashimoto's Food Pharmacology has a recipe list where all meals are part of a low-inflammation diet. These were very helpful for resolving some of my gut issues, and I have since been able to phase some foods back in. Although this book is targeted at thyroid disease in particular, I think the recipes are probably applicable to a wider range of elimination protocols.

Finding a Manageable Baseline

If you're very exhausted and just getting into the habit of making food, a good baseline might be one balanced meal a day that includes a variety of foods, and then the other meals are something simple like eggs on toast and a bowl of oats with fruit and yoghurt. This is fine. The point is that you're not just eating simple carbohydrates and sugars that disrupt your whole metabolic system. The goal is to focus on complex carbs, protein and fat. You can always ramp it up and put more effort into meals over time.

Chronic Pain and the Body

I think chronic pain plays a role in depression. I had bad reactions to a lot of foods, and was in pain often, and when your body is constantly in pain, it's quite difficult to avoid getting depressed.

If you have any repeat sources of pain in your life, you should try and address those, because pain is a signal telling you that something is wrong. I think that ignoring pain signals to your body that you don't care about it, and is a constant reminder that you don't value your own well-being. Common sources of pain that I think a lot of people soldier through include joint pain, dental pain, headaches, menstrual or cyclical pain, ovarian pain, stomach pain, eye strain, or fatigue. Trying to identify what is going on in your body and eliminating sources of suffering is very important.

More broadly, if you have nutritional deficiencies, chronic conditions, or disabilities, these are all contributing factors to depression, and treating them is crucial. I'd suggest trying to rule out hormonal disturbances and other bodily contributing factors as a reason for depression, and treating these factors seriously. Just because a condition is common, or your symptoms are mild in comparison to others, doesn't mean you should just push on and get on with it. If your body has a problem, you should find ways to deal with it and try to create affordances in your life for that difficulty.

For me, this currently means sleep is still a massive priority because my fight-or-flight system seems to get triggered very easily. I don't set alarms because I know I need to provide my body as much of a sense of restfulness as I possibly can, in order to encourage it to be in a restful state — and alarms send a signal of urgency, which is the opposite. For the same reason, I'm quite lenient with myself around food. I aspire toward a keto-style diet, but I also know I need a decent amount of carbohydrates to feel calm, so I don't put pressure on being rigid about it.

Exercise

If you've got the sleep engine and the food engine going — you're roughly getting eight-ish hours of sleep (this might be six, this might be ten, depending on what your body needs) and you're having two to three balanced meals a day — then you want to try and bring exercise into your daily habits.

When you start exercising, do not worry about outcomes. The whole point is to train yourself into having a decent habit.

The way I did this was that I had an agreement with myself that I would move at least every second day — I wouldn't go more than a day without moving, and I would do movement for at least half an hour. Initially, this looked like going to the gym and walking on the treadmill for half an hour, or going for a walk outdoors depending on the weather. I also really liked swimming, so I'd sometimes spend half an hour in the pool. This first form of exercise should be something you have a mild inclination toward, something you actually like, or something that feels like a really low barrier to entry. Walking was a very low barrier for me, as was swimming. But every person is different — if you have other forms of exercise you enjoy, focus on those.

Having this rule in place meant I didn't have to make a decision every day about whether it was an exercise day. I just asked: did I exercise yesterday? If the answer was no, it was an exercise day, and I'd just go and do it.

The other thing that helped was the sunk cost fallacy. If I'd gone to the effort of going to the gym and getting on the treadmill, I'd think, "Well, I may as well try and run a little bit." It wasn't a lot — a couple of minutes doing a little jog and then reverting to walking. But because I was at the gym, I'd think, "I may as well spend a little longer here and try some other things."

As I got more comfortable being in the gym environment, I started trying out different exercises. This built up really slowly — each time I'd add one new thing to the routine. First it was just walking or running, then I tried cycling or rowing, push-ups, squatting. I was careful not to overload myself with new challenges, adding just one of these at a time. After about six months to a year of exercising, I had a full workout going: twenty minutes of cardio, then some squats, pull-ups, and muscle-strengthening activities. But it was really important that I brought this on slow and had very little expectation of outcomes. It was just about showing up.

Doing the Next Best Thing

This was a concept from one of the mental health support groups I attended. The idea is that you don't need to plan out all of the perfect actions for the rest of time. In each moment of your day, if you feel uncertain, you just need to figure out what the next best thing you can do looks like.

So if you're waking up in the morning, you don't need to figure the whole day out. You just need to figure out the next best step. That might be a shower, yoga, a run, eating something, getting dressed, journalling, phoning a friend, phoning your mum. Figure out what is a good thing to start your day with — not doom-scrolling, not eating a donut — figure out what the next thing is that you know will nourish you.

I found this idea really useful because it freed me from having to plan too much, and it also built resilience for adapting to changes throughout the day.

Runway

If you don't have financial runway, you are trapped in your financial situation. I really recommend trying to build up six months to a year's worth of financial runway. Six months is enough for spending some time figuring things out. A year is enough that you can find a job after that period.

It's quite possible to become depressed because you're trapped in a job or study situation that is not actually nourishing you. Runway is really useful because if you can afford to take a couple of months off and explore yourself, a quite likely result is that you won't be depressed anymore and you'll find something more interesting. But this does require quite a lot of active participation and thoughtfulness in how you spend that time off.

Be Like the Wolf: Sleep When You're Tired, Eat When You're Hungry

When I lost my job during COVID I had about six months to a year of runway. This meant that lockdown became a reflective period where I could better attune to my needs. I spent time getting in touch with how my body was feeling and what I needed, without the usual pressures of work or social obligations influencing my decision making so strongly.

I think this laid the groundwork for my proprioception and body-listening practice — the fundamentals of hearing hunger and hearing the need for sleep. At one point my sleep cycle shifted completely — I was awake at three AM and asleep in the afternoon, doing a very weird sleep cycle until it normalised again. But it meant I became in touch with my own rhythm.

Curiosity and the Golden Thread

During my runway period, I also gave myself the freedom to doom-scroll, and I spent a huge amount of time on Twitter exploring what I found interesting and who I related to. By following people on Twitter and getting linked to interesting blog posts, I reconnected with what I find interesting in the world and with what I wanted to work on and the problems I was concerned about. I felt quite active in choosing who I wanted to follow and very aware that I could choose not to follow people or engage with certain types of content. The whole point of Twitter for me was to find people I could relate to and learn from — I found an intellectual peer group. Even though I was quite a lurker and didn't interact a lot, knowing there were other people I found inspiring and relatable out in the world was very encouraging.

One of my really big influences here was Visa (@visakanv), who is quite a prolific writer on Twitter (and more generally on his blog). Finding someone I related to so strongly, who acted as a source of other interesting material, was quite important for rediscovering my curiosity. Something I'd lacked for quite some time was a peer group I felt I related to and wanted to engage with.

Connecting with your drives and curiosities is very useful for building an interesting life that you want to keep living. I think of this as the golden thread. I regularly check in with myself on the extent to which I am following the golden thread, and I pay super close attention to when something feels like a golden thread — being willing to drop everything and chase it down, because I know that if I'm alive and feeling dull, not chasing these threads, this leads to depression. Even if it might be financially less lucrative or a slightly weird choice, I'd much rather follow the golden thread than do something that feels wrong and boring.

So far, this has repeatedly paid off. Last year, I took quite a risk joining a nonprofit when I had a pretty good UX design job lined up and was about to sign a contract. It felt very wrong to be signing that contract, so I put pressure on the possibility of joining the nonprofit instead and was in quite a financially precarious situation for a little bit. But my conviction about that being the right place for me has now paid off, and I'm in a good full-time role that is much more closely aligned with my priorities. I'm not sure if this is just luck, risk tolerance, or a combination of many factors — including having a unique taste in what I think is important in the world.

Relating to Other Humans

I think what's really important for sustained mental health — at least for me — is being surrounded by an intellectually engaged community of earnest, thoughtful people. For others, different types of social activity might be more valuable, eg. group exercise, or family meals. I really value having peers I can talk about interesting ideas with. The ideas part of myself wants to be nourished and loved and interacted with, and doing routine tasks that don't give nourishment to this part makes me feel disengaged and disappointed.

It's important to try and understand yourself and figure out what sort of peer group you need, in what quantity, and at what frequency — because too much social can also be a big burnout factor. Putting pressure on yourself to be an eternally social person is no good either. Figure out the cadence of social you need — whether that's online or offline, in person in big groups or one-on-one.

Conclusion

I started writing a guide like this several times in the past, but kept getting stuck. Finally, one night, I decided to try something different: I used voice-to-text transcription with Claude.[8] I copied the resulting text into Obsidian, and edited it substantially. There were a few things that I was sure were roughly true, and I got Claude to explain them in more detail in the footnotes. This is quite different to how I usually write, but was useful because speaking enabled me to get a lot more onto the page before I got tired. I really wanted to get this out, because I feel myself slipping into a difficult state of mind lately, and I want to make sure I have a record of what has worked in the past, so that I can try and implement it in the future if needed.

Self-reports on health and well-being have been quite useful to me in the past. I don't think it's necessarily the exact interventions that others reference, but rather the way they reason about their struggles. I'm sharing this as a contribution to this type of work that has helped me in the past — I hope it helps someone in the future.
